passage.title: Text One: The Night the River Came In (a modern memoir)
paras: It had been raining for so long that we had stopped talking about it. Then, on the Tuesday evening, the drains began to gurgle backwards, and the grown-ups on our street started to look at the sky in a different way.

My father woke us at two in the morning. He did not shout. He stood in the doorway with a torch and said, 'Shoes on.' That was all. I remember thinking that if he had shouted, I would have been less frightened.

The water was already in the hall. It came in quietly, brown and patient, carrying a single leaf that turned slowly as if it were going somewhere important. The whole house smelt of mud and petrol. We carried my little sister up the stairs in her blanket, and my mother filled the bath with clean water, because nobody knew how long we would be there.

From the landing window, we watched the street become a river. Cars sat up to their windows. Somebody's wheelie bin sailed past like a small, proud boat. Further down, a light went on, then another: everyone was awake now.

What I remember most, though, is not the water. It is Mr Hale from number twelve, who had complained about our football for years, wading across at dawn in his fishing boots with a loaf of bread held high above his head. 'Thought you might need this,' he said, as if he did it every day.

By the afternoon, there were flasks of tea on every wall, and people I had never spoken to were carrying each other's sofas into the sun. The water went down slowly over the next week. The carpets were ruined. The photographs in the bottom drawer were gone.
But some things were found, too. Some of our neighbours never went back to being strangers.

passage.title: Text Two: Letter from a Flooded Valley (in a nineteenth-century style)
paras: To the Editor of the County Herald.
Sir, I write to lay before your readers the condition of our valley, which has been visited by a calamity of which they can have little conception.

The rain, Sir, fell without ceasing for nine days. On the night of the ninth, the river, swollen beyond all memory, broke its banks above the mill and came down upon the lower town with a fury I shall not forget. In the space of an hour it had carried away a cart and its horse's harness, two pigs from the yard of the Red Lion, and the whole of the baker's woodpile, so that there was no fire to bake by on the following morning.

I must, however, record a circumstance which does the highest credit to the labouring people of this place. When the water rose about the cottages by the bridge, where many of the poorest families live, the mill-hands, without waiting for any order, formed a chain across the bridge and passed the children hand to hand to the higher ground. Not one child was lost. These men had worked a full day at the looms; they asked for no reward and received none.
Many families have lost everything they possessed: their furniture, their clothing and their stores of food for the winter. The mill is silent and its people without wages.

I therefore beg, Sir, that you will allow this letter to appeal to the generosity of your readers. Gifts of money, blankets or clothing may be sent to the vicarage, where they will be distributed without delay to those in greatest need.
I remain, Sir, your obedient servant, A Resident of the Valley. October 1866.

head: Q
Question
Marks
rows: From paragraph 1, what made people start to worry?
At what time did the father wake the family?
How does the writer use language and structure to present the experience of the flood?
For how many days had the rain fallen?
Give two things the water carried away.
How does the writer use language and structure to present the people of the valley?

questions.q: From paragraph 1, what made people start to worry?
questions.a: The drains began to gurgle backwards.

questions.q: At what time did the father wake the family?
How does the writer use language and structure to present the experience of the flood?
questions.a: Level-marked: calm 'Shoes on' more frightening than shouting; personified water 'patient', the leaf 'as if it were going somewhere important'; senses 'mud and petrol'; the street becomes a river; structure builds tension to the turn 'What I remember most' and ends on a reflective line.

questions.q: For how many days had the rain fallen?
Give two things the water carried away.
questions.a: Any two: a cart (and its horse's harness); two pigs; the baker's woodpile.

questions.q: How does the writer use language and structure to present the people of the valley?
questions.a: Level-marked: the mill-hands' unprompted courage ('formed a chain across the bridge'); formal praise ('does the highest credit'); contrast with the calamity; the poor families who 'lost everything'; the closing appeal to readers.
